📊 Visa finds 46% in Asia Pacific may use stablecoins by 2031 

📣 Stablecoin interest has moved well ahead of actual use across Asia Pacific, with 46% of surveyed consumers saying they are likely to use the tokens within five years compared with 16% who used them during the past year. The research found strong interest in using stablecoins for online purchases, travel, overseas shopping and moving money across borders. Yet the survey showed a large knowledge gap, with only 6% of respondents demonstrating what Visa described as an accurate understanding of how stablecoins work.

⭐️ Across the 14 markets, 46% of respondents said they were likely to use stablecoins during the next five years. Only 16% reported using them during the previous 12 months. Visa did not disclose in its release what those existing users had used stablecoins for. The 16% figure could therefore include trading, transfers, payments or other cryptocurrency activity and should not be treated solely as consumer payment adoption.

‼️ Cross-border transfers produced one of the strongest future-use readings. Around 49% of respondents said they thought stablecoins could become a common method of moving money between countries within five years. Visa Head of Digital Currencies for Asia Pacific Nischint Sanghavi said consumers were starting to consider stablecoins for “online purchases, travel and cross-border transfers.” The company views those uses as potential extensions of existing payment behavior.

➡️From Vintage to MNTGE: Digital Fashion Brand to Release NFT Patches Linked to IRL Rewards

Digital fashion brand MNTGE is gearing up to release its Patchwork collection, comprised of a series of non-fungible token (NFT) patches paired with a physical counterpart.

MNTGE Patchwork features 13 unique digital patches designed by 11 artists including Jen Stark, Bored Ape Yacht Club artist Seneca and Nyan Cat meme creator Christopher Torres. The entire 7,500-unit collection will open for sale on July 27 on NFT marketplace OpenSea. Each NFT will be priced at 0.07 ETH, or $130, and the artwork will be revealed upon mint.

Each NFT is linked to an identical physical patch. Embedded with a near-field communication (NFC) chip, owners can scan the real-world patch to claim the digital token in their crypto wallet. By holding the patch on the blockchain and IRL, users can trace ownership as well as attend token-gated events and exclusive MNTGE experiences.

Additionally, the patches aren’t just one-off collectibles. In the physical world, they can be sewn onto MNTGE’s “base garments,” including t-shirts, jackets and denim. In the digital realm, the patches can be “owned” by the base garment itself. By implementing an ERC-6551 token standard, the digital wearable becomes a token-bound account that can custody the patches – creating an added layer of digital ownership.

Nick Adler, co-founder of MNTGE, told CoinDesk that the company was rooted in the goal of selling vintage fashion and utilizing the blockchain to revitalize its origins.

“People are out there wearing [vintage] and collecting it…young kids want to be authentic,” said Adler. “They don't want a Hot Topic shirt, they want the original shirt, right? So we just saw this natural, really honest use case for the blockchain, and we just felt like the two could really go hand in hand.”

https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-ngoam-rce-LWKQ4BU?vs_f=Cisco%20Security%20Advisory%26vs_cat=Security%20Intelligence%26vs_type=RSS%26vs_p=Cisco%20Nexus%203000%20and%209000%20Series%20Switches%20NGOAM%20Remote%20Code%20Execution%20Vulnerabilities%26vs_k=1

Multiple vulnerabilities in the Operation, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) feature of Cisco NX-OS Software, known as Next Generation OAM (NGOAM), could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to execute arbitrary code with root privileges or cause a denial of service (DoS) condition on an affected device.
These vulnerabilities are due to improper input validation of IP traffic when NGOAM is enabled. An attacker could exploit these vulnerabilities by sending crafted packets to an IP interface on an affected device. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to execute arbitrary code with root privileges and could cause process crashes, which could result in a reload of the device and a DoS condition.
Note: Feature requirements vary for each vulnerability. For details, see the Vulnerable Products (https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-ngoam-rce-LWKQ4BU?vs_f=Cisco%20Security%20Advisory%26vs_cat=Security%20Intelligence%26vs_type=RSS%26vs_p=Cisco%20Nexus%203000%20and%209000%20Series%20Switches%20NGOAM%20Remote%20Code%20Execution%20Vulnerabilities%26vs_k=1#vp) section of this advisory.
Cisco has released software updates that address these vulnerabilities. There are no workarounds that address these vulnerabilities.

https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-ngoam-rce-LWKQ4BU

🎙 Baqaei reacts to Marco Rubio’s attempt to distort history

📌 Tehran, IRNA – Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei reacted to Marco Rubio's attempt to distort history and construct a philosophical-historical justification for US warmongering.

In response to claims made by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio regarding Iran during a speech in Athens, Greece, on Wednesday, October 7, the Foreign Ministry spokesperson wrote on X:
​
At the Acropolis, Marco Rubio (mis)presents the history of the West - from ancient Greece to the contemporary United States - as a single, seamless continuum. This is the logic of anachronism: a distortion of historical time produced by the careless fusion of categories such as Greece, Rome, Christianity, Europe, America, and, ultimately, “America First.” It is as if America has finally discovered that 'intimidation' can be staged more effectively beneath the neon lights of a philosophy of history than in the bare idiom of the cowboy.
​
Rubio lifts the Greek concept of 'thumos' out of its historical and philosophical setting and recasts it as a celebration of power - of force exercised without law or justice - along with competition and national will. That reading misses a constitutive half of the Greek inheritance. Greece was not only a theater of power and glory. It was also the birthplace of the tragedy of hubris and aggression, from the myth of Troy and Homer’s Iliad; of the critique of imperial ambition in Thucydides’ History of the Peloponnesian War; of political philosophy in Plato’s Republic and Aristotle’s Politics; and of enduring meditations on the limits of power, moral responsibility, and human fate in Sophocles’ Antigone and Oedipus Rex.
​
This other half of the Greek legacy is deliberately omitted from Rubio’s narrative. History is thereby converted from a field of inquiry and critical reflection into an instrument of political legitimation. What emerges is not a philosophy of history, but a manufactured narrative designed to authorize U.S. militancy and to construct a convenient political myth: a distorted reconstruction of the past in which the politics of the present are made to appear inevitable and historically ordained. Once history is pressed into the service of legitimizing power—the unlawful and unjust use of force—its purpose is no longer to understand the past, but to glorify power itself.
​
Vasily Vereshchagin’s The Apotheosis of War offers a stark counter-image. Its pyramid of skulls, left behind by conquerors, confronts the mythology of glory with the material residue of conquest. It recalls what remains when history is reduced to the exaltation of power.
​
At such a juncture, Western thinkers have a responsibility to defend history itself - and the philosophical complexity of Western civilization - against a distorted and apologetic reinterpretation by an aggressive power prepared to sacrifice a civilization’s human achievements in order to legitimize the unrestrained exercise of force.
​
The danger lies not merely in misreading the past, but in appropriating it to authorize that force, and to aggrandize it, in the present.

McDonald’s has rolled out a system that calculates how much people are willing to pay for a specific item.

It looks at millions of orders, competitors’ prices, and how customers respond to price increases. If people at one location are willing to pay more for a Big Mac without hesitation, the algorithm takes that into account.

A real-world example:
At two McDonald’s locations just 3 km apart, a Big Mac can cost $5.69 and $6.89. That’s a 21% difference.

Online retailers are already using the same approach: in the US, in 74% of cases, the same product is shown to different people at different prices.

AI takes into account purchase history, abandoned carts, time spent on a page, even mouse movements, and dozens of other factors.

According to research, personalized pricing is already generating 19% more profit for companies. So it looks like this is what sales will increasingly be built around.
